newsitem.title: UK: ROWING-REDGRAVE TAKES FIRST STROKES TOWARDS SYDNEY.
newsitem.headline: ROWING-REDGRAVE TAKES FIRST STROKES TOWARDS SYDNEY.

text.p: On an uncertain spring day this week under a sun which shone fitfully without raising the temperature, Steven Redgrave took the first smooth strokes towards a fifth Olympic title.
"The train is moving towards Sydney 2000," said German-born coach Juergen Grobler. "It will speed up over the next few days, months, years."
Exhausted emotionally and physically after winning the coxless pairs with Matthew Pinsent in Atlanta last year, Redgrave gave an instant hostage to fortune.
"If anyone sees me near a boat they can shoot me," he said.

Within weeks Redgrave was publicly wavering. Then last November he finally acknowledged that the lure of yet another title was too strong and announced he would attempt to become only the second person to win gold at five consecutive Games.

Two weeks after an emergency appendix operation Redgrave took to the Thames river at Henley, home of the annual regatta, last Tuesday as Britain's new men's heavyweight coxless four rowed together for the first time.
With Pinsent at stroke, Redgrade joined James Cracknell and Tim Foster in the four who will compete for Britain at the World Cup regatta in Munich on May 30-June 1.
Foster, who stroked the losing Oxford crew against Cambridge in the University Boat Race this year, could not resist a sly dig at his distinguished colleague.
"After Steve's comments in Atlanta I hope that anybody who shoots at him doesn't hit me," he said.
Redgrave acknowledged the quip with a brief smile but already he was measuring the effort and time he must expend before the millenium Games.
"My actual strength hadn't diminished," he said in reference to his four-month layoff. "But the endurance levels had really tailed off quite a lot.
"It was very much a point of proving that I was still good enough to be in the four."
Redgrave admitted to only one moment of self-doubt during his first circuit in the gymnasium.
"I found it very tough indeed, halfway through that circuit I though "what the hell am I doing here?'."
If Redgrave's physical strength had temporarily ebbed, his mental toughness has never been in doubt.
He said after his appendix had been removed he had been told by his consultant not to train for three weeks.
"I haven't followed his advice 100 percent," Redgrave confessed to nobody's surprise, adding that he had been working out in the gym and cycling.
Redgrave and Pinsent, very much the senior statesmen in the British quartet, are sponsored by a finance company to the tune of one million pounds sterling ($1.6 million) over the next four years.
The pair, Britain's only real success story at a desperately disappointing Olympics, represent the professional face of their sport.
Elsewhere the British picture remains essentially amateur, reassuring or frustrating according to taste.

The long-haired Foster, who won bronze in Atlanta in the coxless fours, is a student; Cracknell, a qualified geography teacher, had to leave lunch at the Leander Rowing Club early on Tuesday to sign on for the unemployment benefit.

And this weekend the Leander Club will finally vote on whether to admit women members, spurred not so much by belated recognition of sexual equality as by the prospect of 1.5 million pounds ($2.4 million) in national lottery money.
